segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While Apollos was in Corinth, Paul traveled through the inland regions and came to Ephesus. There he found some disciples

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They answered him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “No, we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Into what, then, were you baptized?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Into John’s baptism.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Paul said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “John baptized with a baptism of turning back, telling the people to believe in the one coming after him, that is, in Jesus.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they heard this, they were baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when Paul laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they began to speak in tongues and prophesy.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There were about twelve men in all.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He went into the synagogue and for three months spoke boldly there, reasoning and persuading about the kingdom of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when some became hardened and would not be persuaded, speaking ill of the Way in front of the congregation, he withdrew from them and took the disciples aside, reasoning daily in the lecture hall of Tyrannus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This went on for two years, so that all who lived in Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: God was doing no ordinary works of power through Paul’s hands,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that even face-cloths or work aprons that had touched his skin were carried away to the sick, and their diseases left them and the evil spirits went out.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then some of the itinerant Jewish exorcists also tried to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I charge you by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Seven sons of a certain Sceva, a Jewish chief priest, were doing this.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the evil spirit answered them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Jesus I know, and Paul I know about; but you, who are you?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the man in whom the evil spirit was leapt on them, subdued them all, and prevailed against them, so that they fled from that house naked and wounded.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This became known to all who lived in Ephesus, both Jews and Greeks. Fear fell on them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was held in high honor.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Many of those who had believed kept coming, confessing and disclosing their practices.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: A good number of those who had practiced magic brought their books together and burned them in front of everyone. They added up their value and found it came to fifty thousand silver coins.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So mightily did the word of the Lord grow and prevail.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When these things had been completed, Paul resolved in the Spirit to pass through Macedonia and Achaia and go on to Jerusalem, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “After I have been there, I must also see Rome.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He sent two of those who assisted him, Timothy and Erastus, to Macedonia, while he himself stayed on for a while in Asia.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: About that time there arose no small disturbance concerning the Way.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For a man named Demetrius, a silversmith who made silver shrines of Artemis, brought the craftsmen no little business.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He gathered them together, along with the workers in related trades, and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Men, you know that our prosperity comes from this business,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: and you see and hear that not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a considerable crowd, saying that gods made by hands are not gods.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: The danger is not only that this line of work of ours will fall into disrepute, but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis will be counted as nothing, and that she herself will be stripped of her majesty, she whom all Asia and the world worship.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they heard this they were filled with rage and began shouting,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The city was filled with confusion, and they rushed as one into the theater, dragging along Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians who were Paul’s traveling companions.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Paul wanted to go in among the people, but the disciples would not let him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Even some of the chief officials of Asia, who were friends of his, sent word to him urging him not to venture into the theater.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Some were shouting one thing, some another, for the assembly was in confusion, and most of them did not know why they had come together.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Some of the crowd instructed Alexander, whom the Jews had pushed forward, and Alexander motioned with his hand, wanting to make a defense to the people.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when they recognized that he was a Jew, a single cry went up from them all, and for about two hours they shouted,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the city clerk had calmed the crowd, he said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Men of Ephesus, what person is there who does not know that the city of the Ephesians is temple-guardian of the great Artemis and of the image that fell from the sky?

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Since these things are undeniable, you ought to stay calm and do nothing rash.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: For you have brought these men here, who are neither temple robbers nor blasphemers of our goddess.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So if Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a complaint against anyone, the courts are in session and there are proconsuls; let them bring charges against one another.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But if you are seeking anything beyond that, it will be settled in the lawful assembly.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: For we are in danger of being charged with rioting over today’s events, since there is no cause for it, and we will not be able to give an account of this commotion.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Having said this, he dismissed the assembly.

notes.note: The traditional 'repentance' now suggests mainly feeling sorry. The Greek word, shaped by the prophets' call to 'return' to God, names a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep 'repentance' as an established term that readers understand to include a change of life.

Most translations have 'refused to believe' or 'were disobedient', both of which the verb can mean. It is the negative counterpart of the verb 'persuading' in verse 8, and the rendering keeps that echo: Paul was persuading, and some would not be persuaded.

Acts uses 'the Way' as a name for the movement of Jesus's followers (for example 9:2 and again in verse 23 of this chapter). It was apparently an early self-designation, used before 'Christian' became common.

No Jewish high priest named Sceva is known from other sources. The word can also mean a member of one of the high-priestly families, and some scholars suspect the title was a claim made to impress clients. The matter is uncertain.

The Greek word normally means 'both', which would imply that only two of the seven sons were present. In later Koine it is also found meaning 'all' of more than two, and most translations take it that way here. Either reading is possible.

The word can mean deeds in general, but it was also a technical term for magical procedures or spells. Given the next verse, the believers may be disclosing their spells specifically, which in magical thinking would rob them of their power. The rendering leaves both senses open.

The coin is not named but is probably the drachma, roughly a laborer's daily wage, so the sum is very large. The 'books' are scrolls of spells and formulas; Ephesus had a reputation for such writings.

notes.traditional: purposed in the spirit / resolved in the Spirit
notes.note: The phrase may mean that Paul resolved under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, or simply that he resolved 'in his spirit', that is, made up his mind. Translations are divided. The following 'I must', which in Acts often signals divine necessity, slightly favors a reference to the Holy Spirit.

The Greek title is 'Asiarchs'. These were wealthy leading citizens who held a high office or honorific rank in the province of Asia. Their exact duties are debated; many scholars connect them with the provincial council and its public festivals. That such men were friendly to Paul is notable.

The Greek word here is the ordinary term for a gathering of a city's citizens. The same word names the community of believers elsewhere in the New Testament, where it is traditionally translated 'church'. This translation uses 'assembly' in both settings so the reader can see it is one word. The 'lawful assembly' of verse 39 is the regular, legally convened citizens' meeting, in contrast to this irregular one.

notes.traditional: they drew Alexander out of the multitude / prompted Alexander
notes.note: The sentence is obscure. The verb can mean 'instruct' or 'advise', giving the sense that people in the crowd briefed or prompted Alexander. It can also mean 'conclude', so that some of the crowd concluded Alexander was responsible. Some manuscripts have a different verb meaning 'pushed forward'. Why the Jews put him forward is not stated; perhaps to dissociate their community from Paul.

notes.phrase: temple-guardian of the great Artemis and of the image that fell from the sky
notes.traditional: temple keeper of the great Artemis and of the sacred stone that fell from the sky
notes.note: 'Temple-guardian' was a title of honor that cities claimed, and it is attested for Ephesus in inscriptions. The Greek for the second item is a single word meaning 'fallen from Zeus' or 'fallen from the sky', with no noun attached. It probably refers to a sacred object, perhaps a meteorite or an ancient image, believed to be of heavenly origin; the clerk's point is that it was not 'made by hands'.

In the plural, translators vary between 'miracles', 'mighty works' and 'powers' across the Gospels, Acts and the letters; readers should see one term.
Recurs throughout Acts for Paul's activity in synagogues and halls, and is variously rendered 'reason', 'argue', 'discuss' and 'lecture'.
With the noun παρρησία it runs through Acts, John, Paul and Hebrews, and varies between boldness, openness, confidence and frankness.
